node.label: Antoinette Burton
node.date_label: Burdens of History (1994) · After the Imperial Turn (edited collection) (2003) · Gender History: A Very Short Introduction (2024)
node.description: A historian of Britain and empire whose gender-history intervention treats sexual difference as something produced and managed in historical circumstances. Her account connects gender to slavery, capitalism and empire while distinguishing gender history from simply adding women to existing narratives.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Burdens of History (1994); After the Imperial Turn (edited collection) (2003); Gender History: A Very Short Introduction (2024).

neighbor_nodes.label: Gender history
neighbor_nodes.description: Examines gender as a historically changing organization of social relations, identities and power. Research on work, family, masculinity, bodies and colonial settings connects gender to class, race and other relations without reducing these to one framework. Some feminist historians develop and criticize British Marxist social history; this is one route among several.

strands.focus: Anna Clark’s working-class account and Davidoff/Hall’s middle-class study integrate material relations and cultural meanings differently.

strands.title: Colonial settings and categories
strands.focus: Amadiume’s Nnobi study, Oyěwùmí’s Yoruba argument and Stoler’s colonial analysis cannot be collapsed into one African or postcolonial position.
strands.works: Male Daughters, Female Husbands (1987); The Invention of Women (1997); Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

strands.title: Caste and gendered power

strands.title: Black feminist historiography
strands.focus: Higginbotham’s historical racial analysis and White’s slavery research remain distinct from Crenshaw’s legal argument.

strands.title: Psychoanalytic subjectivity and historical variation
strands.focus: Scott values constructed subjectivity while questioning universal antagonism; her discussion of Alexander identifies a historical feminist use without establishing consensus.

strands.title: Historicizing hierarchical oppositions
strands.focus: Scott’s productive deconstructive use questions fixed binary hierarchies and calls for historical analysis; it is distinct from her criticism of universal psychoanalytic antagonism.
strands.works: Scott, “Gender” (1986), p. 1066

strands.title: Gender within accounts of labor and community
strands.focus: Nair distinguishes recording women’s presence from explaining gendered authority and work. Her questions about a female strike leader, exclusion from paid work and community honor challenge the book’s cultural classifications.
strands.works: Nair review of Rethinking Working Class History (1990), 98

strands.title: Class differences within gender, gender differences within class
strands.focus: Studer explicitly takes up Frevert’s case to oppose treating either class or gender as internally homogeneous. Her broader discussion welcomes analytical differentiation while retaining questions about power and emancipatory purposes.
strands.works: Studer, Überlegungen zu den Kategorien Geschlecht, Klasse und Ethnizität (1993); Frevert, Classe et genre (1991)

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Gender history is a distinct research field with competing explanations and methods. Women’s history remains independent and is not superseded. Racial formation and intersectional analysis have their own entries; connections express specific arguments rather than membership in a combined school. Historical differences of class, race, caste, place and sexuality remain integral questions within gender history.

neighbor_nodes.label: Postcolonial history / critique
neighbor_nodes.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000). Gyan Prakash: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); Stuart Hall: “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’?” (1996); Paul Gilroy: The Black Atlantic (1993). Lauren Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint), selected introduction on colonial difference and jurisdictional politics; contextual contribution, not a common postcolonial doctrine.

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988); A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000); edition with a new preface responding to critics (2007); “In Defense of Provincializing Europe” (2008)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality (1995); treats 'colonizer/colonized' as 'a historically shifting pair of social categories that needs to be explained' (2002, p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); asks scholars to move 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject' (2002). Gouda: homage to her work 'has become de rigueur' in postcolonial studies (2009).
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

representative_people.context: His criticism of idealized and denigrating images of India supplies a specific resource for Guha’s environmental argument. Original article remains to be distinguished from its documented reception.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), especially442, through Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Historian whose essays set out postcolonial historiography from Indian historiography and read Subaltern Studies as postcolonial criticism. His Subaltern Studies context remains distinct.
representative_people.works: “Writing Post-Orientalist Histories of the Third World” (1990); “Subaltern Studies as Postcolonial Criticism” (1994)

representative_people.context: Cultural theorist whose essays on diasporic identity and on the category of the “post-colonial” are standard resources in postcolonial critique. His cultural-studies context remains separate.
representative_people.works: “Cultural Identity and Diaspora” (1990); “When Was ‘the Post-colonial’? Thinking at the Limit” (1996)

representative_people.context: The Black Atlantic criticizes national and racial closure and reads modernity through the Black Atlantic; a standard postcolonial and diaspora text for historians. His Atlantic and diaspora contexts remain.
representative_people.works: The Black Atlantic (1993)

representative_people.context: Coedited Tensions of Empire with Ann Laura Stoler (1997) and coauthored its opening research-agenda chapter. The publisher describes a historical and anthropological inquiry into relations between metropole and colony and changing categories of colonial rule. This contextual inclusion does not identify Cooper as an adherent of every postcolonial theory; his later criticisms require a separate dated claim.
representative_people.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), coedited with Ann Laura Stoler; opening chapter, “Between Metropole and Colony: Rethinking a Research Agenda”

representative_people.context: Metropole and colony in one frame: Birmingham abolitionists, Baptist missionaries and Jamaica, 1830–1867; read as postcolonial history by Woollacott (2006).
representative_people.works: Civilising Subjects (2002)

representative_people.context: Reads the French headscarf ban and the discourse of secularism as civilizational claims about gender equality, in the accounts of her reviewers Laborde and Whitney and her 2018 interview; Laborde finds the normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. Scott asks how to critique secularism without rejecting it (2018 interview).
representative_people.works: The Politics of the Veil (2007); Sex and Secularism (2017)

representative_people.context: Takes Hegel’s World-history to task as a statist frame that, in Guha’s words as Michael quotes them, reached India as an instrument of the East India Company, and asks historians to learn from literature the historicality of everyday life (2002), as Michael and Chakrabarty read the book; Michael fears the state may be lost “as an object of critique” and finds the argument largely conceptual.
representative_people.works: History at the Limit of World-History (2002)

representative_people.context: 'A critical indictment of Western historiography' and of 'history telling as a professional activity' (Craipain, 2024); 'not all narratives or narrators are created equal'. Silencing the Past unread; wording awaits a library copy.
representative_people.works: Silencing the Past (1995)

representative_people.context: Investigates the making of colonial legal authority through cultural classifications, legal intermediaries and competing jurisdictions. Contextual legal history, not adherence to every postcolonial theory.
representative_people.works: “Colonial Law and Cultural Difference” (1999, body unread); Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint, introduction pp. 1–10 read)

representative_people.context: Uses the contact zone to analyze cultural encounter under asymmetrical power rather than presuming coherent, equal communities.
representative_people.works: “Arts of the Contact Zone” (1991); Imperial Eyes: Travel Writing and Transculturation (1992; later second edition separate); Planetary Longings (2022 essay collection).

representative_people.context: Investigates colonial governing power through spatial and administrative arrangements.
representative_people.works: Colonising Egypt (1988; paperback preface 1991)

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Imperial knowledge and cultural authority
strands.focus: Texts acquire authority through institutions and citation; individual writers remain consequential.
strands.works: Orientalism (1978)

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility
strands.focus: Speaking for others and depicting them pose connected political problems.
strands.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

strands.title: Provincializing historical categories
strands.focus: Critique works through inherited concepts without treating Europe as every society’s model.
strands.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

strands.title: Colonial nationalism and difference
strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity
strands.focus: Colonial authority and identification are examined through unstable cultural meanings.
strands.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

strands.title: Feminist difference and coalition
strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.
strands.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984/1991)

strands.title: Race, sexuality and colonial archives
strands.focus: Empire becomes part of the history of European bourgeois sexuality (1995). Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) made 'the intimate' a matter of state and 'colonizer/colonized' a shifting pair of categories (p. 13, as quoted by Ottevaere); the same year her 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' moved 'from archive-as-source to archive-as-subject', the programme now carried by the entry archival_turn.
strands.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995); Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002); 'Colonial Archives and the Arts of Governance' (2002)

strands.title: Critiquing the romanticized East
strands.focus: Guha applies Inden’s critique of hostile and admiring Orientalist images to environmental appropriations of Asian traditions. This documents a particular reception, without making those traditions homogeneous or certifying Inden’s whole argument.
strands.works: Inden (1986), quoted and discussed by Guha (1989),77–78/note9

strands.title: Metropole and colony in a shared research agenda
strands.focus: Cooper and Stoler’s 1997 edited collection supplies a contextual reading on connections between imperial centres and colonial settings and the historical formation of categories of rule. This is the publisher’s description and contents, not a passage-level check or a claim that one programme defines postcolonial history.
strands.works: Tensions of Empire (1997), especially the opening chapter credited to Stoler and Cooper

strands.title: Cultural difference, legal forums and colonial authority
strands.focus: Benton treats legal classifications and forum disputes as elements in making colonial authority. The contests cut across divisions within colonizing and colonized populations. Her selected introduction asks how legal intermediaries and rival authorities altered the terms of rule; it does not treat either side as a coherent legal bloc or turn legal access into a guarantee of justice.
strands.works: Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint), chapter 1 pp. 1–10; “Colonial Law and Cultural Difference” (1999, abstract only).
